label: The paper does not state whether code will be made available, limiting reproducibility.
The method’s novelty is limited because it combines existing approaches rather than introducing a substantially new approach.
The paper should better identify the settings where its method improves on alternatives and its limitations.
The method’s novelty is limited because it mostly repurposes the authors’ NIPS 2015 approach.
The proof of Theorem 1 uses a setting that appears to differ from Definition 3 without explaining why the final bounds remain valid.
Section 3.2.1 does not clearly explain the theoretical results.
The experimental section lacks details needed to understand the experiments and compare them with prior work.
Section 3.3’s title contains a typo.
The paper does not sufficiently explain its contributions or novelty.
The paper is difficult to follow.
The quantization method builds on existing methods, limiting the paper’s novelty.
Notation in Equation 2 is not clearly defined.
Page 4 has a typo: “different” should be “difference.”
The derivation of Equation (8) is unclear.
The last line of Theorem 4.2 contains a typo.
Some notation in Section 3.1 is difficult to follow or used without definition.
There appears to be a typo under Equation (5).
The experimental results are not strong enough.
Section 3.2 uses undefined concepts and needs more intuition, with some technical results moved to the appendix.
Section 3.2 is unclear.
The paper’s presentation and writing need improvement.
Section 3.1 does not clearly describe how the two-stage training approach works.
Theorem 4.1’s fixed labeling function and existentially chosen data distribution make the result too restrictive and potentially tailored to favor over-parametrization.
The paper does not establish whether data augmentation affects the training process or only changes generalization, leaving the observations insufficiently explained.
Section 3.2 and Equation 7 use unclear overloaded notation, with P denoting both the model and the empirical distribution.
Equation 7 does not define R(·,·,·) and P(·,·), or clarify whether they follow Equation 5.
Step 2 of Algorithm 1 is unclear.
Page 4, paragraph 3, has a typo: “used” should be “using.”
Section 2.1 around Equation (2) uses i and j inconsistently.
The paper does not explain the intuition or necessity of the second term in Equation 2, nor compare results with and without it.
The notation for the loss in Algorithm 2 is unclear or unexplained.
Section 3.3 does not sufficiently explain how the proposed method works in practice or demonstrate its implementation.
Theorem 1 requires restrictive bounds on N and I, so its guarantee may not apply to common practical settings.
The equality in Equation 2 is incorrect; it should apparently describe a stochastic approximation of the expectation over q.
The phrase “nontrivialy” on p. 2 is unclear and should be removed or clarified.
The paper does not clearly specify the dimensionalities of its variables and functions.
The paper lacks a concise presentation of the algorithm.
The paper does not clearly disclose that its methods and analyses require full client participation, limiting their applicability to realistic federated-learning settings.
The paper does not explain why its approach outperforms competing methods.
The paper’s presentation is unclear and contains ambiguities that make it difficult to follow.
The paper does not sufficiently position or evaluate its method against recent large-scale single-machine GNNs such as GraphSAINT, L²-GCN, and layer-dependent importance sampling.
The paper does not adequately distinguish its approach from Phan et al. (2018).
The method does not convincingly outperform existing methods and sometimes underperforms them.
The paper does not explain why it uses this Laplacian-network structure, including its softmax-type parameterization.
Section 4.2 is unclear, particularly the equation on page 6.
The paper contains numerous typos and grammatical errors.
The proof of the second part of Theorem 1 in Appendix A.2 is underexplained and vaguely refers to outside papers without specifying which results it uses.
The phrase “theoretical analyses” should be corrected to “theoretical analysis.”
Theorem 2’s proof incorrectly says Lemma 7 is given in Equation (10), and it would be clearer to state the cited Boulle and Townsend result.
The paper contains typos.
The introduction lacks a high-level explanation of the proposed method; a concept figure could clarify it.
The paper does not clearly connect its problem to the cited graph-network works of Battaglia et al. and Kipf et al.
The paper needs experiments on additional datasets.
The related-work discussion omits Cai et al. (ICLR 2017).
Section 4.1 does not clearly explain how action and environment information are disentangled and used.
The paper offers insufficient conceptual or theoretical novelty beyond existing self-training work.
The theorem is limited to linear networks; the paper does not suggest whether it extends to ReLU activation.
The paper omits implementation details needed to clarify the approach and reproduce the results, including the precise architecture and hyperparameters.
Figure 4 does not clarify whether the representation was learned from states or images, or show what it looks like when learned from images.
The paper does not explain why strong regularization helps or how it connects to the prior analysis.
The sentence beginning “Mathematically, the model with learn” has a grammatical error.
The experiments lack comparisons with other baselines.
The evaluation should include ImageNet to test whether the findings hold on a larger dataset.
Equation 1 has unnecessary or unclear universal quantifiers; the exposition should state the Euclidean-space restriction directly.

Theorem 1 gives only a non-diminishing upper bound on the expected gradient norm and does not establish convergence to a stationary point; even the discussed step-size choices yield, at best, convergence to a neighborhood.
The paper lacks comparison with proxy-distribution OOD methods such as Outlier Exposure and energy-based OOD detection.
The related-work discussion should include Belanger et al. (ICML 2017) and Tu et al. (ICLR 2018).
The paper does not explain why adversarial training alone is insufficient for robustness.
The experiments do not convincingly show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches.
The paper lacks a clear motivation for its approach.
The paper does not explain how its results might extend to deep neural networks.
The paper does not clearly establish which of the uniform, L2, and contrastive losses works best or how their effects differ; further analysis is needed to support the loss claims in Section 4.
Section 3.4’s description that COT-trained models “generalized better” needs grammatical reformulation.
The intuition behind Assumption 2 and whether it can be relaxed are unclear.
Section 3.1, Eq. (4), leaves unclear whether 0 represents −1 or a zero-valued weight, making the role of f₂(w) unclear.
The paper does not justify why the original CCA gradient computation is problematic for the proposed goal, given that large minibatches work empirically.
The paper’s contribution appears incremental.
The CIFAR-10 results are substantially worse than previously reported results for the same architecture, and the discrepancy is unexplained.
Figure 1 appears to show the extra-step method’s accuracy decreasing during training, but the paper does not explain this divergence.
Equation 5 does not appear to follow CQL strictly and instead resembles a standard Q-learning loss; clarify the relationship.
Theorem 2 appears to adapt existing results from [2], weakening the paper’s novelty.
The paper does not adequately discuss the implications of its results.
The claim that Proposition 3.2’s scaling law could help extend the analysis to neural networks or other complex models is not explained.
Descriptions of some concepts in the proposed method are unclear.
Figure 2 does not explain what its axes show.
Section 3.2 does not clearly explain how the conditional-distribution fitting objective relates to Equation (1).
The paper should contrast its method with Salimans (2015), particularly the HVI component and whether the reverse model is the main difference.
The paper contains numerous typos and grammatical errors and needs proofreading.
Equation (4) appears to hold only in expectation over p(x), but this is not made clear.
Experiments are limited to MNIST and CIFAR-10; evaluation on a larger dataset such as ImageNet is missing.
The paper does not establish the largest batch size at which the approach remains effective or efficient.
Sections 4.2 and 4.3 overlap with Section 3, making the paper’s organization unclear.
The motivation for the objective in Eq. (6) is not adequately explained.
The paper offers no new machine-learning techniques or generally applicable insights, making its suitability for ICLR questionable.
The experiments do not compare the method with other algorithms.
Key results are relegated to the appendix, making the paper insufficiently self-contained; move them into the main body.
Figures 4 and A.1 should use matching y-axis scales to make their results easier to interpret.
Figure 1B and 1C are unclear, and Figure 1B depicts learned transition vectors as input states without explanation.
The paper’s use of “nonparametric” for neural architectures is potentially confusing and should be clarified.
Results are not strongly favorable overall, especially on ImageNet.
The experiments lack larger-network evaluation, such as ResNet50 on ImageNet, for comparison with state of the art.
The method’s modeling components lack clear motivation, making the approach seem ad hoc.
The paper uses terminology vaguely or inconsistently.
Proposition 3.1, and results relying on it such as Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.1, are not justified for games with agents whose incentives differ.
The paper does not correctly attribute prior work on Transfer Learning, referred to as “fine-tuning” earlier in the paper.
The paper does not explain efficient input and output representations for individual neural-network layers, such as convolution.
Section 4.1 appears to require boundedness of f, but does not state or justify that assumption; Equation 2 may be uninformative if the infimum of f is infinite.
The paper does not make its theoretical guarantees clear.
The comparison omits CAVIA’s ResNet results, which are relevant to the paper’s final ResNet experiment.
The two-hidden-layer architecture may not represent practical deeper models, and the results’ scalability to larger networks is unclear.
The introduction insufficiently motivates applications of the combined explanatory system for image similarity and overemphasizes generalized deep neural networks.
Experiments cover only a few relatively simple environments, leaving performance on Atari and MuJoCo unclear.
The experiments need comparisons with additional baseline methods.
The training procedure is unclear, including whether scene-rotation augmentation and imposed constraints were used.

Calling the method policy optimization is misleading because it learns a confidence set over transition models, making it model-based and inconsistent with the paper’s motivation around practical model-free policy-gradient methods.
The paper does not discuss how its analysis relates to batch normalization or weight normalization.
Important notation is undefined in the paper.
The MNIST experiments are too general and do not closely test the paper's specific claims.
The paper does not show the NAS search process or which architectures were sampled, so it does not establish that NAS favors faster-converging architectures.
The experiments do not evaluate whether the model improves consistently on larger or more complicated datasets.
Figure 2 uses colors that are difficult to distinguish.
The method is limited to binary classification, with no clear extension to multiclass problems.
The paper does not explain how parameter-wise gradient/Hessian updates affect the convergence guarantee or fit the generalized-Adam framework.
The paper does not establish how its exploration method differs analytically and practically from MaxEntRL and inverse reinforcement learning, leaving its novelty and positioning unclear.
Figure 1 is misplaced and should appear in Section 4.4.
The paper does not explain how the approach’s hyperparameters were chosen or tuned.
The reported improvements over the baseline are small.
The paper does not explain how its approach relates to other representation-learning methods.
The paper does not clarify whether ε should be restricted to [0, 1/2].
Section 2.1 gives Y dimensions as R^{D×T}, inconsistent with the paper’s R^{D×T_t} notation elsewhere.
Figure 4 lacks x- and y-axis labels.
The paper does not justify Algorithm 1 or explain why it works.
Table 2 tabular results and Table 3 CIFAR-10 results trail published baselines, but the paper does not explain the comparisons or model-size differences.
The experimental setup, including how datasets are partitioned, models are trained, and results are averaged, is unclear.
Figure 2's caption does not explain the figure adequately.
Figure 3’s caption contains typos.
Figure 1 does not clearly show or explain the number of channels per layer or what the black squares and three blocks represent.
The paper does not convincingly explain how its approach is more easily applied to LSTMs and GRUs than Bayesian deep learning.
The paper does not establish whether the method generalizes to transformer-based models beyond those evaluated.
The SGD comparison does not clarify whether adaptive step-size methods such as Adam were used.
Section 4.3 does not clearly explain or justify how its techniques outperform those in Section 4.2.
The introduction’s related-work discussion detracts from the narrative; a separate related work section may improve organization.
The experimental results lack variance estimates and statistical significance tests.
The paper does not report the model architecture or model size used in the experiments.
The method’s novelty is insufficient because RCNN and concatenated word embeddings are established techniques.
The paper’s writing and structure are difficult to follow.
The paper uses abbreviations before defining them and leaves mathematical variables undefined, including on page 5.
The bolded results in Table 1 are confusing.
The paper does not explain how its computation of gᵀHg differs from prior Hessian-vector multiplication methods or why it is superior.
Figure 1’s results may be driven by stochastic exploration on flat objective regions, making the comparison artificial without step-size adaptation.
The paper does not report how many experimental runs were performed.
The paper does not quantify how repeated inner-loop training affects convergence time versus previous works.
The results lack significance tests.
The claim that the model offers a fundamentally new approach harmonizing neural networks and symbolic program learning is overstated; its human-like hierarchical concept learning is not established.
Reference [2] should cite the NeurIPS version rather than the arXiv version.
The paper omits closely related context-conditional methods, including Ghasemipour et al. (2019) and Wang et al. (2017).
Table 2 is not adequately explained.
The experiments do not compare the method on ImageNet.
The plotted model performances are difficult to compare; the paper should report quantitative results as numbers.

The argument against contrast sets and counterfactual examples is insufficient because the paper has not established that high FIM values reliably indicate classification difficulty or perturbation sensitivity.
The paper does not clearly distinguish its model from clustering or explain theoretically why it differs and is better.
The experimental neural-network architecture, including the final-layer form, is not described.
The paper is too lengthy for its content and approaches the 10-page limit without figures or other material warranting the space.
The related-work discussion omits relevant methods, including LfND, RL with GAN shaping, and Cycle-of-Learning.
Figure 2 is unclear and difficult to interpret.
The paper does not explain why it uses an autoencoder, despite the concern that unsupervised features may underperform discriminative features learned end to end.
Section 4.1 does not clearly specify the training data or regime.
The paper lacks convergence analysis.
Table 1 does not clarify whether baseline results were reimplemented or taken from prior papers, and does not cite sources for reported numbers.
The paper does not explain how the method applies to discrete versus continuous state and action spaces.
The effect of learning rate η is insufficiently demonstrated; Fig. 1 shows only η=0.5 without explanation or comparisons across learning rates.
The paper lacks a clear related-work section.
The references are formatted inconsistently.
Figure 4 is difficult to evaluate because of poor rendering and presentation; the low- and high-resolution ground-truth images are too small for meaningful comparison.
The proposed solutions have limited novelty.
The experiments do not establish whether SVRG improves practical performance or yields higher rewards.
The paper does not establish whether all methods were trained to convergence or report standard and robust train accuracy by class.
Page 7 appears to have a typo: “seminar work” should be “seminal work.”
The paper does not establish whether its methods apply with additive noise or stochastic representations.
Figure captions describe what is shown but do not explain the results or their implications.
The comparison with non-contextual methods is unfair because it uses a non-standard concatenation of word embeddings and average, maximum, and minimum sentence embeddings.

The comparison does not clarify whether prior systems use Transformers or RNNs, how their implementations relate to this paper, whether baseline MLE scores match, or whether hyperparameters were tuned comparably.
The experiments and conclusions are limited to fully connected networks; CNNs are not studied.
The experiments omit a realistic hyperparameter-tuning task for a well-known architecture to demonstrate PrBO against manual search.
The two-sample testing evaluation is not novel.
The simulations should test violations of the assumed model.
Theorem 4’s proof uses the ungrammatical phrase “highly efficient than node clustering methods.”
The paper should define the many-channel limit.
The demonstration-only variant lacks implementation details explaining how Equation 2's weight is computed from state-action samples without querying π^exp.
Assumption 4.1.1 may be incorrectly stated, since it reduces to E f_T <= W_T + E f_0.
Equation 3 may use an incorrect or undefined conditioning range when t = T_p; clarify whether x_[T_p,T_p] should be null.
The experiments need a deeper analysis of how performance changes as the number of available training domains varies.
The robustness of the method to its four hyperparameters is unclear.
The theory assumes access to transition probabilities and reward functions, which are difficult to obtain in complex real-world environments.
Table 1’s reported accuracy is not explained.
The paper does not adequately explain the proposed architectures.
Table 2 compares different architectures, with results partly taken from prior papers and possibly partly retrained, so it does not fairly evaluate the new estimator.
Section 4.2 is missing a period.
The paper does not adequately motivate the proposed pruning technique.
The paper has multiple incorrectly capitalized words, including examples on page 1.
The Introduction contains a typo (“and” in “For instance, and in an attempt to…”) and similar typos elsewhere.
The 20-iteration MultiTargeted test attack may be insufficient; stronger budgets or Croce and Hein’s standard evaluation would strengthen the robustness results.
Figure 2 does not show a significant improvement over competing methods.
The paper has other citation-formatting issues, including places where \citet should be used instead of \cite.
The method is computationally advantageous only in high dimensions, but the manuscript does not establish this case as practically relevant.
Figure 2’s sharp performance degradation beyond a noise-fraction threshold is unexplained, including whether it is expected or due to chance.
The independent-Gaussian assumptions underlying the method are not sufficiently justified.
The comparison may be unfair because existing methods may not have been trained under the paper’s experimental setting.
The paper does not sufficiently explain how a few similar tasks accelerate learning when many distinct tasks are present.
The paper lacks comparisons against quantization and recent pruning techniques.
The paper does not clarify how its experimental training scheme uses the representation for downstream tasks.
The non-Markovian property described before Equation 5 is insufficiently explained, including its implications for dependence on future observations.
Figures 1 and 2 are difficult to read because their fonts are too small.
The paper does not adequately motivate why the framework uses its particular two-pathway encoder-decoder design.
The experiments lack a single baseline with larger hidden layers and a comparable total number of free parameters.
The paper provides insufficient evidence or analysis that its detectors remain robust when an adversary knows about them and adapts attacks.
The proposed optimization method is heuristic and lacks sufficient motivation or theoretical justification.
The attack experiments omit standard white-box baselines such as PGD and C&W, leaving the claimed performance advantage unsupported.
The effect of the reconstruction loss is not evaluated, and the paper lacks an ablation showing whether it can be removed.
The paper does not explain what additional information the learned embeddings capture.
The contribution is incremental because the method heavily follows Prior Networks, and Section 2.1 appears nearly identical to their corresponding subsection.
The paper lacks comparisons with baseline methods.
The paper has missing references.
Section 4 is a loose discussion, and the rigid-body-impact gradients appear relevant only to a subset of the paper’s 2D examples.
The paper does not explain how to choose the hyperparameter p.
The paper lacks provable guarantees supporting its approach.
The paper does not report results across different layer counts to assess whether depth improves performance or causes overfitting.
The experiments lack comparisons with robust reinforcement-learning baselines such as Pinto et al. (2017).
The paper does not adequately clarify which baselines are considered and how they are tuned.
The paper lacks comparisons with state-of-the-art models.
The paper lacks compelling feature visualizations and qualitative experiments beyond Figure 7, including examples of typical learned covariances.
The paper does not explain why Figure 5(a) uses 4 million steps while Figure 5(b) uses 8 million.
The paper does not evaluate whether the method can be combined with adversarial training.
The paper does not explain why the method performs worse or on par in some cases.

Experiments train on random-policy samples or early on-policy samples rather than better-performing offline data, making the training setting unconvincing; the method should also be evaluated on better samples.
The approach should be evaluated in more complex or real-world environments.
Section 4.4 does not clearly explain what is changed in the item-sampling setup.
Table 2 shows little improvement over baselines, and some results are significantly worse.
The conclusion's reported 2.3× training speedup lacks clear support, including a specified baseline and whether it measures per-iteration or total convergence time.
The paper does not compare its method with other methods.
The baseline set is weak: Random and EQUALDIV outperform GRU-supervised, and stronger baselines are needed to assess the paper’s contribution.
The paper does not evaluate alternative approaches, including Wasserstein auto-encoder or InfoGAN-CR, that may disentangle or generalize better.
The results lack confidence intervals in the tables or figures.
The paper does not establish how difficult its task is or whether the approach generalizes beyond its restricted setting.
The claim that the results could improve generalization is unsupported and lacks a citation.
Table 1 lacks comparisons with other methods on its dataset.
The experiments appear to use only 2–3 runs, too few for reliable comparisons given the high return variance.
Sections 3.1–3.2 do not clearly explain how the given reward is used or why it must be known a priori rather than observed during trajectories.
The evaluation covers too few datasets to establish broader performance.
The title overstates the result: pretrained models need substantial symbolic-math fine-tuning to reach quality comparable to symbolic-only training.
The paper does not evaluate whether the approach generalizes to other tasks, such as object detection.
Section 4.2 does not explain its formulation sufficiently for reproducibility.
Without a diversity or uncertainty-promotion term, layer-noise variances may collapse to zero at convergence; the paper does not explain how its training strategy avoids this degeneracy.
The method lacks feature learning, particularly neural-network-based features, that could make it more relevant to ICLR.
The paper does not clarify how task descriptors are used, despite different usages potentially changing task difficulty.
The paper lacks an ablation study of the attention mechanism.
The method is not compared with other approaches, including the related GAN-based methods cited by the reviewer.
Reliance on careful feature engineering may limit the method’s applicability beyond the simple theories studied.
The baseline and proposed method are not tuned thoroughly despite the importance of hyperparameters, making the experimental interpretations difficult.
The evaluation lacks experiments testing robustness across noise levels.
The paper lacks learning curves and ablations showing performance under fewer data, more noise, higher dimensions, or greater system complexity.
The introduction does not clarify the method’s limitation to L_∞ attacks or define a threat model consistent with its poor L_0 results.
The paper does not report how sensitive the results are to different training runs.
The paper does not establish whether the proposed method is optimal or based on a specific model assumption.
The paper does not assess whether the other methods produce reasonable molecules with scores at least as good as its own model.
The baseline results in Tables 1 and 2 are inconsistent, and the discrepancy is unexplained.
The experiments are insufficient to establish robustness beyond dynamically simple problems with easily identified obstacles.
The choice of inputs used to normalize the sampled c_i values is insufficiently justified; robustness may vary across the input space, and sampling near training data may be uninformative.
The paper does not report the ensemble size used in the experiments.
The paper lacks comparisons with newer sequential methods such as Transformer-enabled models.
The paper does not test whether its findings hold with varying amounts of training data.
The paper does not explain why it selected the datasets used in its experiments.
Quality-learning methods such as attention-based approaches are compared with DDL on only one dataset, leaving their effectiveness insufficiently assessed elsewhere.
Table 2 shows only limited performance improvement over the baseline.
The effect of varying the number of pseudo-samples on performance is not reported.
The paper does not explain the proposed method’s benefits over applying DDPG or PPO directly to the problem.
The paper lacks an ablation study.
Because results are close to other approaches, the paper does not establish whether improvements exceed random variation.
The implications of the binary-tree assumption for the transformations produced are insufficiently explained.
The approach may not scale easily, despite the claimed reduction in inference complexity from O(N) to O(log(N)).
The reimplemented LfF model’s BAR accuracy (57.35%) is substantially below the reported 62.98%, and the discrepancy is unexplained.
The method’s dependence on depth maps may make it sensitive to inaccurate geometry and camera poses caused by view-dependent effects, but realistic-data evaluation is limited to Fig. 14.
The baselines are outdated and small-scale; the evaluation lacks comparisons with large-scale cross-lingual models such as the model in arXiv:1901.07291.
The paper does not discuss the limitations of the proposed approach.
The paper does not establish whether the proposed method improves scalability or computation speed.
Experiments are limited to synthetic or small datasets and do not evaluate larger datasets or more complicated models.
The results report reduced FLOPs but omit wall-clock training time, leaving the claimed efficiency unclear on GPUs where sparse computation may not run faster.
The evaluation lacks image-generation metrics such as FID and LPIPS.
Section 2.3 does not adequately justify why noise-induced word permutations help language modeling despite potentially changing sentence meaning and conflicting observations.
The ablation experiments do not adequately disentangle why the proposed method performs better.
Most comparisons use baselines implemented by the authors, which is insufficient to establish effectiveness or close-to-state-of-the-art performance.
The paper neither discusses nor experimentally compares its approach with neural RNN language models.
The experiments lack a running-time comparison, despite the potentially expensive extra computations.
The paper does not report the methods’ time and memory complexity or quantify their impact on training time.
The proposed algorithm appears to rely on hand-crafted rules and instance-specific design, undermining the paper’s motivation that existing OR methods are difficult to generalize.
The evaluation lacks experiments on challenging tasks such as question answering.
The paper does not evaluate how performance changes with different values of K.
The evaluation covers too few environments to show how the method performs across different settings.
The evaluation metric is not adequately explained.
The paper does not adequately explain its contribution to causal inference, especially computing counterfactual probabilities.
